bullets: How steep is a curve at one exact point, and where does the curve turn around?
slides.heading: A-Math differentiation: gradients, the power rule and stationary points
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we learn how to find the gradient of a curve at a single point, differentiate with the power rule and from first principles, find stationary points, and spot the trap that a zero gradient always means a maximum or minimum.

bullets: Find dy/dx as the limit of secant gradients using the power rule and first principles
Find stationary points where dy/dx = 0 and classify them with the sign-change test
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the two goals aloud slowly and tell the class: keep these in mind, because our exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things, including spotting the trap about zero gradients.

bullets: A straight line has one gradient everywhere, but a curve gets steeper and flatter as you travel along it
If the gradient keeps changing, what can the gradient at a single point even mean?
slides.heading: How steep is a curve at one point?
slides.notes: Sketch a curve and ask: the line has one gradient, but this curve does not - so what is its gradient right here, at one point? Take two or three answers, then say: hold them, because the secant closing in on the tangent is the answer.

bullets: dy/dx is the gradient of the tangent at a point: the limit of secant gradients as the two points close in
Power rule: if y = x^n then dy/dx = n x^(n-1) - bring the power down and reduce it by one
First principles: dy/dx is the limit, as h tends to 0, of (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
slides.heading: The derivative is a limit
slides.notes: Say this part slowly, because it is the big idea of the whole lesson: the derivative is not an average gradient between two points, it is what those average gradients approach as the gap shrinks to nothing.

bullets: A secant joins two points on the curve; its gradient is only an average between them
Slide the second point closer and closer: the secant swings round until it becomes the tangent, and its gradient becomes dy/dx
slides.heading: Secant lines close in on the tangent
slides.notes: Point at the animation and narrate what is happening: watch the second point slide along the curve towards the first - the secant line rotates until it just touches as the tangent. That limiting gradient is the derivative.

bullets: Differentiate term by term: bring each power down in front and reduce the power by one
y = x^3 gives dy/dx = 3x^2; y = 5x^2 - 4x gives dy/dx = 10x - 4; a constant differentiates to 0
slides.heading: The power rule
slides.notes: Work down the terms one at a time and watch each power drop: the 3 comes down and x^3 becomes 3x^2. Then ask the class to call out the next one before you reveal it.

bullets: Start with the secant gradient (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h for y = x^2: it simplifies to 2x + h
Let h tend to 0 and the secant gradient becomes 2x - the same answer the power rule gives, now proved
slides.heading: dy/dx from first principles
slides.notes: Follow the algebra as the h terms cancel: the secant gradient 2x + h still has the gap h inside it, and only when h tends to 0 does it become the exact gradient 2x.

bullets: Where the tangent is horizontal, dy/dx = 0: these are the stationary points
Classify by the sign change of dy/dx: positive to negative is a maximum, negative to positive is a minimum, no sign change is a point of inflexion
slides.heading: Stationary points: max, min, inflexion
slides.notes: Trace the tangent as the curve climbs, flattens at the top and falls: at the flat moment dy/dx is 0. Then walk the signs either side - plus to minus means the top of a hill, a maximum.

bullets: The trap claim is: dy/dx = 0 means a maximum or minimum.
Watch y = x^3 at x = 0: the gradient falls to 0 but the curve keeps climbing - stationary, yet neither maximum nor minimum
slides.heading: Stationary is not always max or min
slides.notes: Name the trap out loud before anyone falls into it: zero gradient only says the tangent is flat for an instant. Watch the curve pause at the origin and climb straight through - that is a point of inflexion, not a turning point.

bullets: Step 1: for y = x^3 - 3x, dy/dx = 3x^2 - 3 = 0 gives x = 1 and x = -1
Step 2: sign test - at x = -1 the gradient changes positive to negative (maximum, y = 2); at x = 1 negative to positive (minimum, y = -2)
slides.heading: Worked example: find and classify the stationary points
slides.notes: Talk through the two steps slowly and name each one as you write it; say: first solve dy/dx = 0 for the stationary points, then let the sign change either side do the classifying - never guess from the zero alone.

bullets: Differentiate y = 2x^3 - 6x and find its stationary points, classifying each with a sign test
Careful - a classmate claims: dy/dx = 0 means a maximum or minimum. Explain to them why that is wrong, using y = x^3
slides.heading: Your turn: differentiate, then classify
slides.notes: Give pairs three minutes, then cold-call two pairs: listen for the trap - dy/dx = 0 means a maximum or minimum. The fix is: Stationary is not always max or min: check the sign change. y = x^3 at x = 0 is stationary and still climbing.

bullets: On your own: differentiate y = x^4 and state the gradient at x = 2
Watch out for the trap one last time: dy/dx = 0 means a maximum or minimum. Say what extra check a stationary point needs
slides.heading: Exit ticket: prove it before you leave
slides.notes: Close by reminding the class of the trap - dy/dx = 0 means a maximum or minimum. - and the fix: Stationary is not always max or min: check the sign change. y = x^3 at x = 0 is stationary and still climbing. Collect the tickets as they leave and check who still classifies by the zero alone.
